definitionsAndCoreConcepts: The transtheoretical or stages-of-change model treats intentional behaviour change as a staged and potentially iterative process rather than a single event.
Precontemplation describes a stage in which there is no current intention to change the target behaviour.
Contemplation describes recognising or considering the case for change without yet taking action.
Preparation describes intending and planning to act in the near future.
Action describes active modification of the target behaviour.
Maintenance describes sustaining the changed behaviour and managing the risk of relapse.
Termination describes a state in which the target behaviour is no longer desired and temptation to return is absent or very low.
modelsResearchAndRelationships: The stages describe different readiness states and can guide the type of support that is appropriate at different points in behaviour change.
Relapse or movement between stages means the model is better understood as dynamic than as a guaranteed one-way progression.
evaluationAndLimits: The six-stage model should not be taught as a rigid ladder through which everyone progresses once and in the same order.
Termination is less commonly reached or emphasised in some applications, so maintenance and relapse management remain important practical endpoints.
misconceptionsAndBoundaries: Being aware of a problem does not by itself place someone in the action stage.
Relapse does not invalidate the model; movement backwards or renewed cycling can occur.
The stages describe readiness for change rather than guaranteeing successful behaviour change.

revisionSynthesis: The exact AQA naming is retained only as board alignment. The teaching structure is independently authored from the accepted open evidence.
